What, exactly, are the basal ganglia optimizing? In the most classical reinforcement-learning formulation, the basal ganglia optimize policies so as to maximize expected cumulative reward: they adjust the probability, timing, and vigor of actions according to whether those actions lead to better-than-expected or worse-than-expected outcomes.

Thus, unlike the cortex, which minimizes precision-weighted prediction error over a high-dimensional generative model, the basal ganglia optimize a family of behaviorally consequential objectives defined over policy selection, policy execution, and policy timing. Their core problem is not to construct a richly structured world model, but to evaluate candidate actions defined over cortical state representations and to bias behavior toward those expected to improve future outcomes. Those “actions” should be understood broadly: not only overt motor outputs, but also covert cognitive and affective operations; value appraisals can be computed over inferred latent states, predictive state representations, and other cortex/hippocampus-supplied features [Dopamine reward prediction errors reflect hidden-state

inference across time; What is dopamine doing in model-based reinforcement learning?]. In that sense, the basal ganglia are best understood as the brain’s principal policy optimizer, embedded in cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops that channel limbic, associative, and sensorimotor information into competitive selection and dopaminergic credit assignment 1, 2, 3. In active-inference language, one can say that cortex supplies much of the state space and predictive structure, whereas basal ganglia help convert preferences over outcomes into biases over policies, thereby helping steer both overt and covert action toward preferred states of the world 4, 5, 6.

The scalar RPE as the canonical BG loss

To optimize a policy one needs a training signal that evaluates how well current action selection is doing. In the basal ganglia, that signal likely derives from the Bellman consistency condition, which defines the value of a state as the expected immediate reward plus the discounted value of its successor:

V(s)=𝔼[r+γV(s′)]\begin{equation} V(s)=\mathbb{E}[r+\gamma V(s')] \end{equation} If the agent’s value estimates are correct, successive predictions should agree. The temporal-difference (TD) error δ=r+γV(s′)−V(s)\begin{equation} \delta =r+\gamma V(s')-V(s) \end{equation} measures the violation of this agreement at each time step 7, 8. Here, δ\delta does double duty. Minimizing 𝔼[δ2]\mathbb{E}[\delta^2] trains the value function (the "critic"), but the sign and magnitude of δ\delta simultaneously provide the gradient information the system needs to adjust the policy (the "actor"): a positive δ\delta stamps in whichever action or context preceded it, a negative δ\delta stamps it out, and zero δ\delta leaves the current policy unchanged. It is this dual role that makes a single scalar error sufficient to drive policy optimization over arbitrarily large action spaces–the BG need not represent a full error vector over every possible action, but only broadcast whether the most recently selected action turned out better or worse than expected.

A large body of evidence identifies the phasic activity of midbrain dopamine neurons with precisely this TD error signal. Dopamine neurons produce bursts following unexpected rewards, transfer their phasic response timing from the unconditioned stimulus to reward-predictive cues with learning, and pause at the time of expected but omitted rewards—each observation conforming quantitatively to the TD prediction error 8, 9, 10, 11. Causal manipulations (e.g. optogenetic activation or inhibition of dopamine neurons timed to reward events) produce behavioral changes consistent with the TD learning algorithm, confirming that δ\delta is not merely correlated with learning but plays a causal role in driving it 12, 13, 14. The upshot is that the phasic dopamine broadcast constitutes a policy-relevant loss signal: it is the error term whose iterative minimization reshapes striatal action-selection weights toward an improved policy. A recent striatal model links dopamine-dependent plasticity and direct/indirect pathway activity to action selection and reinforcement learning (Figure) 94. A recent striatal model links dopamine-dependent plasticity and direct/indirect pathway activity to action selection and reinforcement learning (Figure).

Average-reward formulation and policy timing/vigor

The discounted-return framing captures how basal ganglia learn which action to select, but a policy is defined not only by choice but also by timing, vigor, and threshold. In continuing, free-operant, or self-paced settings an average-reward formulation brings these additional policy dimensions into focus. Here the relevant baseline is not discounted future value but the long-run average reward rate ρ\rho, and the error term takes the differential form

δ=r−ρ+V(s′)−V(s)\begin{equation} \delta =r-\rho+V(s')-V(s) \end{equation} The policy-optimization interpretation is immediate: ρ\rho represents the opportunity cost of time. When average reward rate is high, every moment spent deliberating, waiting, or moving slowly is a moment that could have been spent collecting reward; the optimal policy therefore responds faster, moves more vigorously, and lowers its effective decision threshold. When ρ\rho is low, the opportunity cost of time drops and a more cautious, energy-conserving policy is preferred. In this way the average-reward formulation extends the BG’s policy-optimization mandate from the content of action (what to do) to its dynamics (when to do it, how hard, and at what evidence threshold), linking reinforcement-learning theory to literatures on vigor, latency, effort allocation, and urgency 15, 16, 17.

The average-reward account should nevertheless be stated with some care. It remains influential, and there is convergent evidence that dopaminergic function is related to reward-rate-dependent invigoration and to reduced decision thresholds during reinforcement learning, but the field has not converged on a simple one-to-one identification of tonic dopamine with ρ\rho. Recent human and animal work is more consistent with a broader picture in which dopamine contributes jointly to learning, action selection, movement vigor, and reward-rate-sensitive control, without forcing those roles into a single literal coding interpretation. A clean synthesis, then, is that the two formulations carve up the same policy-optimization problem along complementary axes: the discounted TD formulation best captures how the BG learn state and action values to determine the content of choice, whereas the average-reward formulation best captures how they regulate the temporal envelope—tempo, vigor, threshold—within which that choice is executed. These are most productively treated as complementary slices through a single effective loss landscape rather than as mutually exclusive theories 18, 17, 19.

Actor-critic models of the striatum

In reinforcement learning, the actor-critic architecture factors the policy-optimization problem into two coupled subproblems: a critic that learns a state-value estimate V(s)V(s), and an actor that learns a policy π(a∣s)\pi(a∣s) over actions 7. Importantly, the critic’s value estimate is not an end in itself–it exists to enable computation of the TD error δ=r+γV(s′)−V(s)\delta =r+\gamma V(s')-V(s), which then serves as the training signal for both modules. The critic uses δ\delta to correct its own value estimates (minimizing 𝔼[δ2]\mathbb{E}[\delta^2]), while the actor uses the sign and magnitude of δ\delta to reinforce or suppress whichever action preceded the outcome (ascending the expected-return surface). The value estimate thus sits at the root of the entire optimization: if the critic is inaccurate, the TD error is noisy, and the actor’s policy updates are correspondingly degraded. The architecture is "shared-error, asymmetric-role": a single scalar δ\delta trains both modules, but it is the critic that makes δ\delta possible in the first place. A review illustrates reward prediction errors (Figure) 95. The review illustrates iterative reinforcement learning (Figure).

A longstanding hypothesis maps this factored architecture onto striatal anatomy: the ventral striatum (particularly the nucleus accumbens) serves as the critic, and the dorsal striatum serves as the actor 20, 1. The proposed computational flow is as follows. Ventral striatal neurons learn state-value estimates through cortical, limbic, and thalamic afferents. Those value signals are communicated–via ventral striatal projections to the ventral pallidum and thence to midbrain dopamine nuclei–to the circuitry that computes δ\delta 21, 22. Dopamine neurons then broadcast the resulting TD error to both ventral and dorsal striatum simultaneously 23. In ventral striatum, δ\delta drives critic learning–refining the value estimates from which future errors will be derived. In dorsal striatum, the same δ\delta drives actor learning–adjusting action-selection weights so that policies associated with positive surprise are reinforced and those associated with negative surprise are weakened. The ventral striatal value estimate therefore "trains" dorsal striatal policy not through a direct ventral-to-dorsal projection, but through its foundational role in shaping the dopaminergic error signal on which both systems depend. The figure reports additional results from the cited study (Figure).

Several lines of evidence support this division of labor, if imperfectly. Action-preference and chosen-action signals are reliably found in dorsal striatum but are weak or absent in ventral striatum 24, 25, 26, 27, consistent with an actor role. Ventral striatal activity, conversely, tracks state value and reward expectation in a manner consistent with a critic 28. And dopamine projections to both regions carry quantitatively similar TD error signals, as the architecture requires 23. The dissociation sharpens under manipulations that isolate the two roles: ventral striatal responses appear whenever reward is predicted–under Pavlovian as well as instrumental contingencies–whereas dorsal striatal responses emerge specifically when an action must be learned to procure that reward 28, precisely the double dissociation the partition predicts, since value prediction is demanded in both settings but policy learning only when behavior is instrumental. Lesion and inactivation work converges: disrupting dorsal–especially dorsolateral–striatum preferentially impairs the acquisition of stimulus-response habits while leaving reward prediction and outcome expectancy comparatively intact 29, an actor-selective deficit. The mapping also has an anatomical substrate for the ventral-to-dorsal flow it presupposes: striato-nigro-striatal projections in the primate are organized as an ascending spiral, in which ventral striatal sectors influence midbrain dopamine populations that project back to slightly more dorsal territory, and so on in an open, feed-forward cascade from shell toward dorsolateral striatum 30–exactly the directional, serial connectivity the critic-trains-actor story requires, with the value-carrying ventral sectors sitting upstream of the action-selecting dorsal sectors within the dopaminergic loop rather than the two being symmetrically coupled. The figure reports additional results from the cited study (Figure). A 2025 analysis examines the basal ganglia output bottleneck (Figure) 99. The analysis models how basal ganglia output can control cortical dynamics (Figure).

The division is nonetheless imperfect in the ways one expects of a heuristic mapped onto biology. Action-value and chosen-value signals are not strictly confined to dorsal striatum–they appear, more weakly, in ventral territory in some tasks, and state-value signals are readily recorded dorsally–so the actor/critic boundary behaves as a gradient rather than a partition 26. More fundamentally, whether the dopaminergic teaching signal is the pure state-value error δ\delta of a textbook actor-critic, or an action-value error closer to SARSA or Q-learning, remains unsettled: dopamine activity has been shown to track the value of the upcoming, about-to-be-chosen action rather than state value alone, which the strict critic-teaches-actor scheme does not straightforwardly predict 31. The architecture is thus best read as a well-supported first-order description–critic ventral, actor dorsal, shared dopaminergic error–onto which the biology layers overlap, graded transitions, and an open question about exactly which error the system computes.

From scalar to distributional: the BG loss is richer than a single mean

The classical TD account treats the basal ganglia as learning a single expected return: the critic estimates the mean future value of a state or action, and phasic dopamine reports the scalar error relative to that mean. But when outcomes are stochastic, the mean is only one statistic of practical relevance. A policy may care not only about expected payoff, but also about dispersion, downside risk, upside potential, and the temporal profile with which rewards arrive. In distributional reinforcement learning, the learned object is therefore not just the scalar value V(s,a)=𝔼[Z(s,a)]V(s,a)=\mathbb{E}[Z(s,a)], but the full return distribution Z(s,a)Z(s,a) itself. Computationally, this is achieved by maintaining a family of parallel value predictors with different asymmetric sensitivities to positive and negative prediction errors, such that different channels converge to different quantiles or expectiles of the outcome distribution rather than all collapsing onto the mean. From a loss-function perspective, this reframes the BG objective as something richer than minimizing a single mean-squared TD loss: the system instead minimizes a coordinated set of asymmetric regression losses whose collective solution approximates the full distribution of future returns 32, 33, 34. A review distinguishes several dopamine signal patterns (Figure). The review illustrates reward maximization through prediction errors (Figure).

This moved from an attractive AI analogy to a serious biological hypothesis when Dabney and colleagues showed that dopamine neurons are not perfectly redundant copies of one scalar RPE. Instead, individual dopamine neurons displayed stable heterogeneity in their reversal points (i.e where neurons shift from signaling above baseline for high-value rewards to below baseline for low-value rewards) and in the relative scaling of positive versus negative prediction errors, precisely the pattern expected if different channels were learning different expectiles of the reward distribution 33. Decoding from this heterogeneous population recovered multimodal reward distributions that standard mean-based TD learning cannot represent. On this view, the dopaminergic teaching signal is still an RPE, but not a single homogeneous number in any literal circuit sense; it is better described as a structured population of distributional RPE channels, spanning more optimistic and more pessimistic forecasts of future reward 33, 32. A primate study examines diverse value estimates in anterior cingulate cortex (Figure) 100. The study examines asymmetric prediction-error responses (Figure).

More recent work has pushed this story downstream into the striatum itself. In a task that dissociated reward mean from reward variance, Lowet and colleagues found robust abstract encoding of variance in striatum, showed that chronic ablation of dopamine inputs disrupted these distributional representations without abolishing mean-value coding, and further found that D1 and D2 medium spiny neurons preferentially encoded the right and left tails of the reward distribution, respectively. That result is especially important for a basal-ganglia loss-function section, because it suggests that the direct and indirect pathways may participate in an opponent distributional code: not merely “Go” versus “NoGo” around a single scalar value, but optimistic versus pessimistic slices of the return distribution that can support sensitivity to uncertainty and risk. In that sense, the BG loss may be biologically implemented as a vector of partially opponent objectives over the distribution of possible outcomes, rather than as one scalar error around one scalar prediction 35.

That said, this should still be framed as a strong emerging account, not as settled biology. For instance, recent work shows that dopaminergic heterogeneity can also be explained by feature-specific prediction errors, where heterogeneity arises because different dopamine neurons receive different state-feature inputs rather than different asymmetric scaling factors 36. The two frameworks are not mutually exclusive; they likely address different sources of heterogeneity (outcome-specific asymmetry versus input-specific projection topography), and a complete account of the BG loss landscape may require both 36, 35. In addition, changes in tonic dopamine levels can shift the balance of D1- versus D2-receptor sensitivity and thereby induce population-level optimistic or pessimistic biases in value learning–a mechanism complementary to the phasic-response asymmetries that underlie distributional coding at the single-neuron level 37. What can be said with increasing confidence is that the BG loss signal, once idealized as a single scalar δ\delta, is better understood as a structured, heterogeneous population code whose individual components minimize different members of a family of asymmetric loss functions, and whose aggregate output supports both the expected-value computations required for standard policy optimization and the distributional computations required for a richer, more adaptive relationship with uncertainty.

RL across timescales

The frontier picture is richer still, because the relevant distribution appears to extend over time as well as reward magnitude. Classical TD learning compresses all future rewards into a single scalar value through one fixed discount factor γ\gamma, and therefore through a single temporal horizon: a single value of γ\gamma implies a single answer to the question "how far into the future should the agent care?" But animals must assign credit and select actions across an enormous range of timescales–from sub-second motor adjustments during a song or a reach to multi-hour foraging expeditions–and a single discount factor cannot accommodate this range without either myopically ignoring distant rewards or slowly blurring the distinction between cues that predict reward at different delays 7, 38. Multi-timescale RL proposes that the brain maintains a family of parallel TD learners, each operating with a different discount factor γi\gamma_i, so that the dopaminergic teaching signal is not a single scalar δ\delta but a structured vector of prediction errors spanning short to long planning horizons 38, 39, 40.

At the level of dopamine release within the striatum, this idea receives striking anatomical support. Mohebi, Wei, and colleagues simultaneously recorded dopamine transients in the dorsolateral (DLS), dorsomedial (DMS), and ventral (VS) striatum of rats performing instrumental and Pavlovian tasks, and found that dopamine dynamics systematically accelerated from ventral to dorsomedial to dorsolateral striatum across three functionally distinct measures: the tempo of spontaneous dopamine fluctuations, the time constant over which prior reward history was integrated to form predictions, and the rate at which cue-predicted future rewards were discounted 41. In a multiple-delay Pavlovian task, dopamine responses to cues predicting reward at 0.6, 3, and 12 seconds showed the steepest discount in DLS and the shallowest in VS, with DMS intermediate–and a recurrent neural network model with three pools of LSTM units at τ\tau=2s, 10s, and 1,000s reproduced the distinctive subregional response profiles, including weak DLS cue responses (because the cue-predicted reward is too temporally distant for a short-horizon learner), sluggish VS cue discrimination (because a long-horizon learner pools value across many trials), and sharp DMS discrimination (because its intermediate horizon best matches the trial-length timescale of the Pavlovian task) 41. This topographic gradient maps naturally onto the known hierarchical organization of cortico-basal ganglia loops, in which ventromedial striatum participates in limbic circuits that organize behavior over long timescales, dorsomedial striatum in associative circuits for cognitive control, and dorsolateral striatum in sensorimotor circuits for rapid, habitual responding 42, 43, 44. For the BG loss function, this gradient means that the effective discount factor γ\gamma entering the TD error δ=r+γV(s′)−V(s)\delta =r+\gamma V(s')-V(s) is not a single system-wide constant, but varies topographically across striatal subregions, so that each cortico-basal ganglia loop effectively minimizes a different temporal slice of the Bellman consistency condition. A rat study records dopamine across striatal regions (Figure). The study compares reward-history timescales across the striatum (Figure).

The same logic applies at the level of individual midbrain dopamine neurons. Masset, Tano, and colleagues recorded optogenetically identified VTA dopamine neurons in mice performing a cued-delay reward task and a virtual-reality approach task, and found robust heterogeneity in the discount factor γ\gamma across individual neurons: some neurons responded strongly only to cues predicting the shortest delay, while others showed gradually decaying responses across much longer delays 39. Single-neuron discount factors were best fit by exponential (not hyperbolic) decay functions, were stable across random trial splits, and were correlated across the two tasks, indicating that the temporal discount factor is a cell-specific property of individual dopamine neurons rather than a context-dependent parameter 39. This diversity has a powerful computational consequence: by applying a regularized inverse Laplace transform to the population vector of cue responses (each weighted by the neuron’s fitted γi\gamma_i), Masset and colleagues could decode the probability distribution over future reward times from a single snapshot of the population response–a computation that is mathematically impossible from a single-timescale scalar value 39, 34. In simulations, agents equipped with multiple discount factors outperformed single-timescale agents at disentangling reward magnitude from delay, at converting between exponential and hyperbolic discount functions, and at inferring reward timing even before value learning had converged–capabilities that are ecologically essential but inaccessible to a homogeneous δ\delta 39.

Published simultaneously with the Masset et al. study, Sousa, Bujalski, and colleagues extended this framework to the joint distribution over reward time and magnitude. In their time-magnitude RL (TMRL) model, individual dopamine neurons are characterized by two heterogeneous parameters: a discount factor γi\gamma_i (governing temporal sensitivity) and an asymmetric RPE scaling parameter κi\kappa_i (governing sensitivity to reward magnitude, as in the distributional account discussed above). Combining these two axes of heterogeneity, the authors showed that just 450 ms of the dopamine population response to a reward-predictive cue was sufficient to decode a two-dimensional probabilistic "map" of future reward over both "when" and "how much" 45. The decoded reward-time predictions correlated with trial-by-trial anticipatory licking, suggesting that this distributional temporal code is not merely epiphenomenal but is actually used to guide the timing of behavior 45. Moreover, the TMRL model predicts–and the data confirm–that the distribution of discount factors across neurons adapts to reward statistics in accordance with efficient coding principles: when the longest-delay cue was removed from the task, neurons shifted their discount factors to devote more coding resolution to short delays, and vice versa 45.

For a BG loss-function account, the multi-timescale picture has three major implications. First, it means the BG loss landscape is not parameterized by a single γ\gamma but by a spectrum of discount factors distributed across both striatal subregions and individual dopamine neurons, so that the effective objective being optimized at any given level of the cortico-basal ganglia hierarchy is 𝔼[δ2]\mathbb{E}[\delta^2] for a circuit-specific γi\gamma_i. Second, when combined with the distributional account (asymmetric RPE scaling across neurons), it implies that the dopaminergic teaching signal carries not just the expected value of future reward but something approaching its full joint distribution over time and magnitude–a far richer error signal than the original scalar δ\delta, and one that can support risk-sensitive, time-sensitive, and state-dependent policy optimization 45, 39. Third, the observation that individual dopamine neurons carry stable, cell-intrinsic discount factors that correlate across tasks constrains the biological implementation: the spectrum of temporal horizons appears to be built into the midbrain itself, perhaps through molecular or circuit-level heterogeneity in dopamine neuron properties, rather than being flexibly reassigned trial by trial 39. Taken together, the distributional and multi-timescale extensions do not displace the classical TD account of the BG loss but unfold it: what was once idealized as a single scalar error minimizing 𝔼[δ2]\mathbb{E}[\delta^2] around a single discounted value is better understood as a structured population of errors, distributed over both reward-magnitude quantiles and temporal horizons, whose collective minimization shapes a policy that is sensitive not only to expected payoff but to its full probabilistic landscape in time. Dopamine responses to reward-predictive cues differ by region (Figure). A model tests temporal discounting across regions (Figure).

Territory-specific objective functions

The preceding subsections traced the BG loss from its scalar TD origin through distributional and multi-timescale extensions; taken together, these analyses suggest that the dopaminergic teaching signal is far richer than a single number minimizing a single 𝔼[δ2]\mathbb{E}[\delta^2]. The present subsection asks: what representations does δ\delta operate over, in which striatal territories, and how does this vary across the parallel cortico-basal ganglia loops? Answering this question is essential because the effective objective function optimized by any given BG circuit depends jointly on (i) the state representation feeding into the value estimate, (ii) the temporal horizon of the prediction, and (iii) the behavioral domain the loop controls. The "many worlds" hypothesis of dopamine prediction error captures this intuition: because the basal ganglia are organized as a set of parallel circuits, each receiving distinct cortical inputs and projecting to distinct downstream targets, the same formal TD error may carry qualitatively different information in different loops–different "worlds" of prediction 46. Recent anatomical work has further refined this picture, revealing that the mouse cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic network comprises at least six parallel subnetworks–limbic, associative, and multiple somatomotor channels–each of which transduces a specific subset of cortical information through every elemental node of the loop and relays thalamic output back to the originating corticostriatal neurons in a bona fide closed loop 47. These loops, however, are not hermetically sealed: open-loop projections, particularly from ventral striatum through medial SNr to motor thalamus, allow limbic information to exert a unidirectional influence on motor cortical output 48, providing a circuit-level mechanism by which motivational and affective evaluations can bias action execution.

Within this anatomical framework, the basal ganglia can be understood as implementing territory-specific objective functions: each striatal territory, embedded in a particular cortico-basal ganglia loop, optimizes a partially distinct behavioral objective using dopaminergic δ\delta computed over a loop-appropriate state representation. We can sketch this territory-by-territory as follows.

Ventral striatum / limbic loops. The ventral striatum—particularly the nucleus accumbens core and shell—sits within limbic cortico-basal ganglia loops linking infralimbic, prelimbic, orbitofrontal, and insular cortices with mediodorsal and ventromedial thalamus 49, 50, 44. Its dominant objective is to evaluate states in terms of motivational value, incentive salience, and homeostatic relevance, and to gate the initiation of approach or avoidance policies under affective and interoceptive control. Dopamine RPEs in ventral striatum are the best-characterized in the literature and exhibit the canonical pattern: bursts to unexpected reward, transfer to reward-predictive cues, and pauses at reward omission 8. Value signals here reflect the subjective motivational significance of predicted outcomes, integrating information about reward magnitude, probability, delay, and—in the distributional account—the full shape of the outcome distribution 33, 35. In the multi-timescale framework, ventral striatal dopamine dynamics operate on the longest temporal horizons, integrating reward history over many trials and reflecting the shallowest temporal discounting 41. In active-inference terms, ventral striatum helps convert prior preferences over outcomes into the expected free energy computations that bias policy selection toward preferred states 4.

Dorsomedial striatum / associative loops. The dorsomedial striatum (roughly, the primate caudate head) receives input from prefrontal, anterior cingulate, and parietal association cortices and participates in loops through mediodorsal and ventral anterior thalamus 49, 2, 44. Its dominant objective is flexible, goal-directed action selection: learning which action produces which outcome under current task contingencies and updating that mapping when contingencies change 51, 28. Dopamine RPEs in dorsomedial striatum track action-outcome contingencies, show sensitivity to model-based value computations, and operate on intermediate temporal horizons 41, 23. Lesion and inactivation studies confirm that the dorsomedial striatum is necessary for goal-directed behavior that is sensitive to outcome devaluation and contingency degradation 51. A human drug study investigates exploration and exploitation (Figure) 97. The study tests dopamine drugs and exploratory choice (Figure).

Dorsolateral striatum / sensorimotor loops. The dorsolateral striatum (roughly, the primate putamen) receives input from primary motor, premotor, and somatosensory cortices and projects through ventrolateral thalamus back to motor cortical areas 49, 2, 44. Its dominant objective is the compilation and execution of well-practiced action sequences—skills, habits, and automatized motor programs that are relatively insensitive to immediate outcome devaluation 52. Dopamine dynamics here are the fastest, integrating reward history over the fewest trials and reflecting the steepest temporal discounting 41. Strikingly, dopamine signals in dorsolateral striatum are positively shifted relative to other regions: reward responses remain non-negative even for outcomes worse than expected, and clear inhibitory "dips" to negative prediction errors are absent or strongly attenuated 23. This positive bias means that the effective teaching signal in dorsolateral striatum preferentially stamps in actions that were at least minimally successful, without erasing them when outcomes occasionally fall short—a property that may explain why dorsolateral-striatum-dependent behaviors are resistant to extinction and insensitive to devaluation, the hallmarks of habit 23.

Tail of the striatum / posterior sensorimotor territories. The tail of the striatum receives input from visual and auditory association cortices and is innervated by a distinct population of dopamine neurons that respond to novel and salient sensory stimuli with opposite initialization compared to ventral striatum–showing excitation rather than the typical inhibition to novel cues 53, 54. These posterior dopamine neurons have been shown to reinforce avoidance of threatening stimuli and, in recent work, to support value-free repetition biases and action-prediction-error signals, suggesting a role in stabilizing stimulus-action mappings distinct from canonical value-based learning 55, 56, 57. A 2025 mouse study tests the tail of the striatum in action learning (Figure). The study measures posterior-striatal dopamine during movement (Figure). The authors compare signals with action-prediction-error models (Figure). The study tests whether posterior-striatal dopamine reinforces actions (Figure).

Importantly, this territory-specific architecture again implies that the BG do not gate only overt motor actions. Through associative and limbic loops, the basal ganglia also gate cognitive operations–including attentional set-shifting, working-memory updating, and the selection of internal cognitive strategies. In active-inference accounts, these covert operations are themselves "actions" selected under the same policy-optimization logic that governs overt behavior: the basal ganglia bias which cortical content gains access to downstream processing, and dopaminergic δ\delta trains these gating policies just as it trains motor ones 5, 6, 42. The ventral and dorsomedial loops, in particular, are positioned to gate prefrontal representations that determine what cognitive "policy" is currently active–whether to maintain a working-memory trace, switch attentional focus, or retrieve a new goal from long-term memory.

On this view, the basal ganglia are best regarded as comparatively shallow evaluative and gating circuitry sitting downstream of richer cortical and hippocampal computations. Recent work increasingly supports a division of labor in which cortical inputs to striatum carry belief-like or predictive representations, and corticostriatal plasticity learns the mapping from those representations to values and action preferences; in recurrent-network terms, the striatum may function as the final readout stage of a deeper value-approximation architecture rather than as the site where the full task model is explicitly constructed 3, 58. This framing preserves what is distinctive about basal ganglia function–their role in evaluation, competitive gating, and dopaminergic credit assignment–while dissolving the misleading claim that they are intrinsically "model-free". What differs across ventral, associative, and sensorimotor loops is how rich the incoming state representation is, how far into the future it predicts, and what behavioral objective that territory is trying to optimize.

From raw rewards to subjective utility

The reward term in the basal ganglia’s TD objective should not be interpreted as raw physical payoff. What matters for action selection is the subjective utility of an outcome: the internally transformed desirability of reward after amount has been warped by the organism’s preferences, uncertainty attitude, temporal discounting, effort costs, reward type, and current physiological state. In that sense, the dopaminergic teaching signal is better described as a utility prediction error than as an error over objective reward amount. A useful shorthand is

δtu=u(ot)+γVu(st+1)−Vu(st)\begin{equation} \delta_t^u=u(o_t)+\gamma V^u(s_{t+1})-V^u(s_t) \end{equation} where u(ot)u(o_t) denotes the subjectively transformed outcome and VuV^u is a value function expressed in utility coordinates. This is the right computational interpretation if the basal ganglia are to optimize behavior rather than merely track stimulus physics 59, 60.

A broad body of work supports this stronger reading. Dopamine prediction-error responses integrate subjective value across multiple reward dimensions rather than encoding any single physical attribute in isolation: in monkeys, responses follow revealed-preference value integrated from reward amount, risk, and reward type, even when options cannot be ranked on any single objective scale 61. Reward delays similarly reduce dopaminergic cue responses in parallel with behavioral temporal discounting 62. And physiological need can rapidly revalue an outcome, with mesolimbic dopamine updating accordingly, as when sodium depletion turns hypertonic salt from aversive into appetitive 63. Taken together, these results imply that the teaching signal received by striatal plasticity is already expressed in behaviorally meaningful value units rather than in raw sensory units.

The most direct formal evidence comes from experiments that estimated utility functions explicitly. Stauffer and colleagues derived nonlinear utility functions from monkeys’ risky choices and showed that dopamine reward responses followed the marginal utility of reward—that is, the local slope of the utility function—rather than simple reward magnitude 64. More recently, Hill and colleagues used an auction-like task to obtain trial-by-trial measures of instantaneous subjective value, and found that dopamine neurons tracked fluctuations in bids even when the physical reward was held constant; conversely, similar bids for different reward amounts elicited similar dopamine responses 65. These results are especially important for a loss-function account because they show that the dopaminergic error signal follows the animal’s momentary internal valuation, not just its long-run average preference over objective outcomes.

The newest evidence pushes this further from “utility” in the narrow sense toward subjective prospect value. Ferrari-Toniolo, Seak, and Schultz showed in 2026 that primate dopamine neurons nonlinearly code both reward magnitude and probability, and that the population signal integrates utility with subjectively weighted probability in a way that closely matches each animal’s revealed choices 66. In parallel, single-neuron recordings across reward circuitry—including dorsal and ventral striatum—have shown prospect-theory-like coding in which neuronal activity is captured by a multiplicative combination of utility and probability-weighting functions, not merely expected value 67. Thus, under uncertainty, the relevant BG objective may be not merely expected reward 𝔼[r]\mathbb{E}[r], nor even classical expected utility pu(m)pu(m), but a subjectively transformed prospect value w(p)u(m)w(p)u(m), in which both reward magnitude and reward probability are nonlinearly warped by the organism’s preferences.

For the basal ganglia, the conceptual consequence is straightforward: the scalar RPE is not “about reward” in any naive physical sense. It is about whether the obtained or expected outcome was better or worse than anticipated in the organism’s own subjective currency. That currency can incorporate risk attitude, delay, effort, physiological need, reward identity, and even distortions of probability itself. Crucially, this subjectivity is not constructed within the basal ganglia in isolation. Midbrain dopamine responses are shaped by the rich cortical and cortico-hippocampal representations that feed into the dopaminergic system—representations that already embed inferred latent states, contextual structure, predictive beliefs, and other consequences of a generative world model. In that sense, dopamine does not merely report the value of a physically specified reward, but the value of that outcome as interpreted through a model-based, inference-laden representation of the situation. The basal ganglia therefore learn policies that maximize subjective utility—or, under uncertainty, subjective prospect value—over the state space furnished by cortex. The strongest direct evidence for this claim comes from relatively simple appetitive and risky-choice tasks, so one should be cautious about overextending it to all forms of abstract or social valuation; but as a description of the loss term driving dopaminergic teaching and corticostriatal learning, “subjective utility” is now a much better approximation than “objective reward amount,” precisely because the dopaminergic error itself is already informed by a rich generative model of the world 59, 65, 66, 68, 69, 70. The same study compares reward-based prediction errors (Figure). The authors test the contribution of orbitofrontal inputs (Figure).

Constraints and regularizers on the BG loss

The canonical BG objective is often written as the maximization of expected discounted or average reward, but that idealization is too thin for the biology. A better description is that the basal ganglia optimize a constrained or regularized policy objective: candidate actions are evaluated not only by their expected payoffs, but also by their energetic and opportunity costs, their representational complexity, their fit to current physiological need, and the circuit-level requirement that commitment be sparse and mutually consistent. Importantly, these constraints need not appear as separate explicit symbols in a single dopaminergic scalar. In the brain they can enter by reshaping state representations upstream of the BG, by altering local dopamine release within striatum, and by changing how BG output nuclei regulate competition and threshold. On this view, the effective BG loss is not “maximize reward” in the abstract, but “maximize constrained subjective utility” 71, 72, 73, 74.

A first and probably most central regularizer is effort and energetic cost. Across motor and cognitive domains, recent reviews converge on the idea that striatal dopamine helps compute net utility rather than raw benefit alone, biasing control toward options whose expected gains justify their costs 71, 72. In influential computational interpretations of BG opponency, this cost-benefit balancing is implemented by partially opponent pathways: direct-pathway activity emphasizes prospective benefits, whereas indirect-pathway activity emphasizes countervailing costs, risks, or losses, so that BG output approximates a net-action score rather than a pure reward score 73, 74. This does not mean that D1 neurons are literally “benefit neurons” and D2 neurons literally “cost neurons” in every context; the biology is more mixed than that. But as a loss-function summary it captures an important truth: corticostriatal plasticity is trained toward actions whose returns exceed their costs, not toward actions with maximal reward magnitude irrespective of expense. Consistent with that framing, nucleus accumbens D2R neurons carry signals about prior unfavorable outcomes and can bias subsequent risky choice toward safer options, suggesting that loss- and cost-like information enters directly into the policy update machinery 75.

At the same time, effort is not always just a subtractive penalty. Recent work shows that the relationship between cost and value can be path-dependent: striatal dopamine release reflects not only reward magnitude but also sunk cost, meaning that the reward response can be amplified by how much has already been invested 76. A striking 2026 extension showed that in the nucleus accumbens, high-effort rewards evoke rapid local acetylcholine release, which then augments reward-evoked dopamine via nicotinic receptors on dopamine axons; blocking this cholinergic amplification selectively blunts dopamine release in high-effort contexts and impairs effortful behavior while sparing low-effort consumption 77. The implication for a BG loss-function account is subtle but important: effort sometimes acts as a regularizer that discourages costly actions ex ante, but once effort has been expended it can also revalue the obtained outcome ex post, increasing commitment to the hard-won reward. Thus “effort cost” is not only a penalty term subtracted from reward; in some contexts it is folded back into the reward term itself. A 2026 preprint compares forms of striatal dopamine transmission (Figure) 98. The preprint tests locomotion and learning after altered dopamine release (Figure).

A second regularizer is policy complexity. Real animals cannot implement arbitrarily rich state-action mappings, so policy optimization is constrained by finite informational and memory capacity. Resource-rational RL formalizes this as a compression cost on the policy—often expressed as the mutual information between states and actions—which penalizes overly specific mappings even when they would increase reward 78. In mice, behavior in a perceptual decision task lay close to the optimal reward-complexity frontier, and the same work found that midbrain dopamine responses to reward outcomes were suppressed by policy cost, consistent with the idea that phasic teaching signals themselves may incorporate a complexity penalty 78. This is especially relevant for a BG chapter because it suggests that dopaminergic learning may be regularized not only by what an action earns, but by how expensive it is—in an informational sense—to maintain the policy that produces it. Put differently, the BG may favor policies that are good enough and compressible over policies that are slightly better but too brittle, high-dimensional, or memory-hungry to implement robustly. How such a penalty is implemented is an open question, but it need not be hard-wired. A plausible implementation is that the regularizer is itself learned: rather than optimizing against a fixed complexity coefficient, the system may acquire an inductive bias toward compressible policies from the statistics of experience—an Occam’s razor discovered rather than imposed—together with an implicit self-model as a compute- and memory-bound agent for whom cheap, robust policies tend to transfer. On this view the complexity cost need not be computed by a dedicated module but can be folded directly into the teaching signal, consistent with the observation that dopamine responses are suppressed for costlier policies 78. A preprint models policy complexity as a constraint on learning (Figure). The preprint relates policy cost to mouse dopamine responses (Figure).

A third class of constraints is homeostatic and allostatic. From this perspective, the BG do not optimize reward in a vacuum; they optimize actions with respect to the organism’s current bodily needs and predicted future internal states. In homeostatic reinforcement learning, the rewarding value of an outcome is defined by how much it reduces deviation from an internal setpoint, making reward intrinsically state dependent 79. More recent modeling has pushed this directly into BG terms by proposing that physiological state rescales dopaminergic teaching signals and, as covered in "From raw rewards to subjective utility", that the relevant prediction error is an error over utility, not objective reinforcement, where utility depends on both outcome and need 80. The sodium-appetite literature provides a concrete demonstration: homeostatically regulated RL models can reproduce both state-dependent choice behavior and the corresponding modulation of nucleus accumbens dopamine responses by sodium deprivation and satiety 81. A recent review generalizes this logic still further, arguing that primary rewards are generated by interoceptive processes and are fundamentally dependent on internal states and goals, so classical RL must be extended to explain how those state-dependent reward signals are themselves generated 82. For the BG loss, the upshot is that physiological need is not a side variable sitting outside the objective; it helps define the objective in the first place.

A fourth regularizer is selection itself: the basal ganglia do not merely score actions, they impose sparse commitment under conflict and uncertainty. In computational terms, the STN-GPe-GPi circuitry can be viewed as adding a penalty against premature, impulsive, or mutually incompatible action selection, effectively raising the amount of evidence needed before commitment when conflict is high. This idea has long been formalized as an STN-mediated increase in decision threshold or “hold your horses” signal 83, 84. Recent recordings and modeling sharpen that picture: human BG recordings show that theta dynamics in STN, GPe, and GPi differentially shape a collapsing decision boundary as a function of conflict and uncertainty, with STN theta associated with slower boundary collapse and thus more deliberate choice in high-conflict settings 85. Complementing this, 4-Hz STN stimulation in Parkinson’s patients increases decision threshold, whereas standard ~130-Hz stimulation decreases it 86. These findings imply that part of the BG objective is not about reward magnitude at all, but about how and when commitment occurs: the system regularizes policies toward temporally appropriate, non-impulsive selections that respect competition among alternatives.

Taken together, these results suggest that the most useful formal summary of the BG loss is not a bare reward term, but something like expected subjective utility under cost, complexity, physiological, and commitment constraints. Some of these constraints warp the reward term itself—for example when internal state changes the utility of an outcome, or when expended effort amplifies the dopamine response to a reward. Others act more like classical regularizers on the learned policy—for example by penalizing excessive policy complexity or by raising decision thresholds under conflict. This richer picture does not displace the TD/RPE framework; it specifies the kind of value function the TD machinery is actually learning. The scalar or population-level dopaminergic error remains the teaching signal, but it is computed around a value landscape that has already been reshaped by body state, cortical inference, local striatal modulation, and BG selection dynamics. In that sense, the basal ganglia do not optimize raw reward; they optimize a biologically feasible, organism-relative, and circuit-regularized approximation to long-run utility 71, 78, 81, 85.

Relationship between BG loss and cortical loss

The cortical and basal-ganglia loss functions are best understood as complementary rather than competing objectives. Cortex is primarily organized to reduce high-dimensional, precision-weighted prediction error—more generally, variational free energy—so as to infer latent causes, learn structured world models, and refine sensorimotor predictions. The basal ganglia, by contrast, do not mainly learn by reconstructing the sensory stream itself; they learn by assigning value to policies defined over the state representations that cortex, hippocampus, and other systems make available. Put simply, cortex is optimized for epistemic adequacy—“what state am I in, and what is likely to happen next?”—whereas the basal ganglia are optimized for pragmatic adequacy—“given that inferred state, which policy should be selected, energized, timed, or suppressed?” The difference is therefore not just one of anatomical locus but of computational object: cortical losses are locally factorized mismatches over features, levels, and timescales, whereas BG losses are comparatively low-bandwidth evaluative signals—classically TD/RPE-like errors—that say whether the current policy was better or worse than expected 87, 88, 3, 4. A 2025 mouse study examines prediction errors beyond reward (Figure) 96. The study measures dopamine during sensory preconditioning (Figure).

This division immediately clarifies why basal-ganglia learning can look strikingly “model-based” even if the BG themselves need not house a full generative world model. Dopaminergic and striatal evaluative errors are often computed over inferred states rather than raw observations. Hidden-state inference, contextual disambiguation, task structure, and belief-state estimation can all be carried out upstream by cortical, orbitofrontal, hippocampal, and prefrontal circuits; the BG then evaluate those inferred states using TD-like machinery. In that sense, the sophistication of the BG loss landscape is representation-dependent. A richer cortical state space gives the basal ganglia a richer object over which to compute subjective utility, risk, temporal horizon, and action value; a poorer cortical state space makes the very same dopaminergic machinery look more purely “model-free.” The crucial point is that much of the apparent model-basedness of BG optimization is imported through cortical state construction rather than generated de novo within the striatum 68, 69, 70, 19.

The relationship is not merely serial but recurrent. Cortical inference determines the state features over which basal-ganglia value functions and action preferences are learned, but BG output feeds back through thalamocortical loops to regulate which actions, task sets, attentional allocations, working-memory gates, and internal operations are actually disinhibited. The BG therefore do not simply read out a value from a finished cortical model; they help determine which trajectories through state space the organism will actually traverse. By selecting a saccade, a reach, a retrieval policy, or a cognitive set, the BG alter the future sensory samples the organism receives and therefore alter the subsequent cortical prediction errors available for learning. Cortex and BG are thus better described as a coupled optimizer pair: cortex constructs and updates the predictive state space, while the basal ganglia compress that space into policy biases, vigor settings, and commitment signals that determine how the agent samples the world next 46, 3. A mouse study tests dopamine signals for sensory predictions (Figure). The study tests specificity of learned cue associations (Figure).

In an active-inference vocabulary, this complementarity can be stated even more tightly. Cortical losses are naturally formulated in terms of variational free energy and its forward-looking extension, expected free energy, which score both current model fit and the anticipated epistemic and pragmatic consequences of future policies. Within that broader architecture, the basal ganglia can be understood as implementing a comparatively low-bandwidth policy-selection and policy-precision mechanism embedded within a larger cortical generative model. Cortex—especially temporally deep hippocampal and prefrontal circuitry—contributes the hidden-state model and predicted outcome landscape; dopaminergic/BG circuits help transform those predictions and preferences into competitive biases over executable policies. On this reading, classical RPE-based BG losses are not alien to cortical free-energy minimization. They are one biologically efficient way of approximating the evaluative part of policy optimization once a cortical generative model has already furnished the relevant state space and predicted consequences 89, 4, 90.

The boundary, however, is functional rather than absolute. Dopamine is not only a corticostriatal teaching signal; it also modulates cortical processing, and cortical circuits in turn help shape dopaminergic responses through state inference, uncertainty estimation, and model-based prediction. The cleanest synthesis, then, is not that cortex “learns” while BG merely “choose,” but that cortex and BG implement distinct yet reciprocally nested loss functions. Cortex primarily minimizes errors of representation, prediction, and uncertainty over a structured generative model of the world. The basal ganglia primarily minimize errors of valuation, policy selection, timing, and commitment over the states that model provides. The former builds the space of possibilities; the latter assigns actional significance to that space. Together they form a two-level optimization architecture in which world-model learning and policy learning are analytically separable, but biologically inseparable in operation 91, 92, 93.
